title: Sprints
description: The shortest races are also the simplest to understand and the hardest to master. From the blocks to the line, a sprinter has seconds to get everything right: a clean start, a powerful drive phase, and a relaxed top speed held to the finish. The 100 metres is the signature event, but the family runs from indoor 60 metres to the full-lap 400, where pacing joins power. What separates good sprinters from great ones is rarely effort; it is technique held together at maximum speed, when the body wants to tighten up. Train the start, train the speed, and train the calm.

topics.History: Sprints have anchored athletics since the first modern Olympic Games in 1896, with the 100 metres as the best-known race in the sport.
topics.Rules: Lane discipline applies across the sprint distances, false starts cost the race, and timing goes to hundredths of a second.
topics.Techniques: The start, the drive phase, and relaxed speed are the three phases to train. Tension is the enemy at top speed.
topics.Training: A week mixes starts, short accelerations, top-speed runs, and strength work, with full recovery between hard efforts.

demo.code:

TIME_S = 48.0
print("400 metres pace example")

print("Pace per 100 m: %.1f seconds" % (TIME_S / 4.0))
print("Pace per 200 m: %.1f seconds" % (TIME_S / 2.0))

title: Middle-Distance Running
description: The middle distances are where tactics and fitness collide. At 800 metres the race is two laps of controlled aggression; at 1500 metres it is nearly four laps of positioning, surges, and a final kick. Runners must be fast enough to sprint and fit enough to sustain it, and the best ones also read races: when to lead, when to sit, when to move. Sit too far back and the kick never reaches the leaders; lead too early and the field runs past in the straight. Training teaches the body to hold race pace while tired, which is the whole event in one sentence.

topics.History: The middle distances grew from nineteenth-century mile racing into the Olympic 800 and 1500 metres, keeping their tactical character.
topics.Rules: The 800 metres breaks from lanes after the first bend; the 1500 metres starts from a curved line with open positioning.
topics.Techniques: Pacing, pack position, and kick timing decide races. The runner who moves at the right moment beats the runner who moves earliest.
topics.Training: Race-pace intervals, tempo runs, and speed sessions build the blend of speed and endurance the events demand.

demo.code:

print("Pace per 1000 m: %.1f seconds" % (TIME_S / 1.5))

title: Long-Distance Running
description: Long-distance running is the art of staying relaxed at speeds that should not be sustainable. The track events are 5000 and 10000 metres, and the road and country versions add hills, mud, and weather. Races are usually patient: even pacing, small surges, and a finish that only looks like a sprint because everyone is tired. The training is equally patient, built on daily mileage, one long run, and tempo work that teaches the body to hold a strong effort. Economy is everything; the runner who wastes least wins most.

topics.History: Distance racing has anchored athletics since the early Olympic Games, with road and cross-country traditions running alongside the track events.
topics.Rules: Waterfall starts and open positioning govern track distance races; road races use mass starts on measured courses.
topics.Techniques: Stride economy, even pacing, and relaxed form under fatigue decide results. Surges test rivals without spending the race.
topics.Training: Mileage, long runs, tempo efforts, and intervals form the weekly pattern, with recovery days protecting the load.

print("Laps: %d, pace per lap: %.1f seconds" % (25, TIME_S / 25.0))

title: Hurdles
description: Hurdling is sprinting with obstacles, and the obstacles punish every technical flaw. Each race has ten hurdles: the short races are flat-out sprints over barriers, and the 400 metres version adds fatigue and stride management. The technique is a rhythm: a fixed stride count between hurdles, a fast lead leg, a trail leg snapped through low, and a body that stays low over the barrier. Hit a hurdle and it falls forward, costing time; run around one and the race is lost on rules. The best hurdlers look like they are barely hurdling at all.

topics.History: Hurdle racing grew from obstacle races into standardised Olympic events with ten hurdles per race.
topics.Rules: Hurdles are built to fall forward. Striking one costs time; avoiding one or deliberately clearing them away breaks the rules.
topics.Techniques: Rhythm is everything: a set stride count, a quick lead leg, a fast trail leg, and minimal time in the air.
topics.Training: Drills, rhythm runs, sprint work, and mobility training build the pattern until it survives fatigue.

demo.code:

HURDLES = 10

print("Average gap between hurdles: %.1f m" % (DISTANCE_M / HURDLES))
print("Stride pattern example: 15 strides early, 17 late as fatigue changes stride length")

title: Steeplechase
description: Add solid barriers and a water pit to a distance race and you get the steeplechase: 3000 metres, 28 barriers, and seven water jumps. The barriers do not fall, so runners must clear them cleanly, and the water jump rewards those who step on the barrier and drive far past the pit. It is a hybrid event: part distance race, part hurdling, part obstacle negotiation. Rhythm matters most; a runner who fights the barriers wastes the energy needed for the final lap. The race usually comes down to who is still smooth after the last water jump.

topics.History: The event takes its name from cross-country races run between church steeples, later standardised to 3000 metres on the track.
topics.Rules: Twenty-eight barriers and seven water jumps must be cleared. Stepping on barriers is allowed; bypassing them is not.
topics.Techniques: Smooth barrier clearance and a long water-jump landing save time and energy. Rhythm between obstacles is the key skill.
topics.Training: Distance work, hurdle drills, and repeated water-jump practice build the hybrid fitness the event needs.

title: Relays
description: Relays turn individual speed into a team skill. Four runners, one baton, and exchanges inside a marked zone: that is the whole event, and it is where medals are won and lost. In the sprint relay the exchanges happen at full speed, with the outgoing runner moving before the baton arrives. In the longer relay there is more time, but the runners are tired, which makes clean exchanges harder, not easier. A dropped baton or an exchange outside the zone ends the race on rules. The best relay teams practise exchanges until they are automatic.

topics.History: Relays joined the Olympic programme in the early twentieth century and became the team centrepiece of every major championships.
topics.Rules: The baton must change hands inside the zone. Drops, out-of-zone exchanges, and lane infringements can disqualify a team.
topics.Techniques: Timing the outgoing runner's start, taking the baton without looking, and ordering legs by strength decide results.
topics.Training: Exchange drills under pressure matter as much as sprint training; teams rehearse until exchanges are automatic.

title: Marathon
description: The marathon is 42.195 kilometres of patience. The legend behind it is a messenger's run from Marathon to Athens; the reality is months of training distilled into one morning. Fuel is the hidden contest: stored energy runs low after about 30 kilometres, so runners drink and eat on the move and pace to survive the final stretch. Start too fast and the last ten kilometres punish every early second gained. Mass races now welcome tens of thousands of runners, but the event's logic never changes: respect the distance early, and it may respect you late.

topics.History: The event recalls a legendary run to Athens, entered the first modern Games in 1896, and settled at 42.195 kilometres.
topics.Rules: Certified measured courses and mass starts govern road marathons, with timing mats along the route.
topics.Techniques: Pacing discipline and mid-race fuelling decide marathons. The runner who saves energy early has it late.
topics.Training: Long runs, tempo work, and careful recovery build over months; the longest training runs usually stop short of race distance.

title: Race Walking
description: Race walking looks simple and is anything but: one foot must stay on the ground, and the supporting leg must stay straight until it passes beneath the body. Judges watch every athlete, and warnings accumulate into disqualification. The speeds surprise newcomers; elite walkers cover 20 kilometres in well under 90 minutes without ever visibly running. The technique is a hip-driven stride with rapid turnover, and it breaks down under fatigue, which is exactly when judges watch hardest. It is a discipline of form held together for hours.

topics.History: The discipline grew from pedestrian contests into Olympic racing, keeping its two defining rules: contact and a straight supporting leg.
topics.Rules: Judges enforce contact and leg-straightness rules. Repeated violations bring disqualification.
topics.Techniques: Hip drive, straight-leg action, and quick turnover generate speed legally. Form under fatigue is the deciding factor.
topics.Training: Long walks and drills build the stride; strength work supports the hips and legs through long races.

title: Long Jump
description: Sprint, take off, fly, land: the long jump turns runway speed into distance. The measurement runs from the take-off board to the nearest landing mark, so accuracy at the board matters as much as speed. In the air, jumpers use hang or hitch-kick techniques to stay balanced and set up a feet-first landing that falls forward, protecting every centimetre. Cross the board and the jump fouls, however far it goes. Several attempts per competition mean a jumper can build through rounds, but the best legal jump is the only one that counts.

topics.History: Jumping for distance is among the oldest athletics events, present at the first modern Games in 1896.
topics.Rules: The board is the line: take off behind it or the jump fouls. Measurement goes to the nearest mark left in the sand.
topics.Techniques: Speed on the runway, precision at the board, balance in the air, and a forward landing all add distance.
topics.Training: Sprint work, take-off drills, bounding, and strength training build the jump.

demo.code:

legal = [a for a in ATTEMPTS if a > 0]
print("Legal jumps: %s" % legal)
print("Best jump: %.2f m" % max(legal))
print("Average legal jump: %.2f m" % (sum(legal) / len(legal)))
demo.expected_output:
Long jump series example (0 = foul)
Legal jumps: [7.82, 7.95, 8.02, 7.9, 8.1]
Best jump: 8.10 m
Average legal jump: 7.96 m

title: Triple Jump
description: Hop, step, jump: three phases, one continuous movement, and a landing in the sand. The triple jump used to carry its old name openly, and the name still describes it perfectly. The skill is balance between phases: a hop that is too long wrecks the step, and a step that is too long wrecks the jump. Speed matters, but rhythm matters more, because the phases must flow without braking. Measurement matches the long jump, from board to nearest mark, and board fouls cost jumps. It is the most technical of the horizontal jumps.

topics.History: The event dates to the first modern Games in 1896 under its older name, the hop, step, and jump.
topics.Rules: The sequence is fixed: hop, step, jump. Board fouls do not count, and measurement goes to the nearest sand mark.
topics.Techniques: Balanced phases and unbroken rhythm win. Overreaching on the hop destroys the phases that follow.
topics.Training: Bounding, phase drills, sprint work, and strength training build the rhythm and power the event needs.

print("Best jump: %.2f m" % max(legal))
print("Improvement from first to best: %.2f m" % (max(legal) - legal[0]))

title: High Jump
description: Run a curve, plant one foot, and arch backwards over a bar: the high jump's modern technique, the Fosbury flop, won Olympic gold in 1968 and changed the event forever. The trick is physics: by arching head- and shoulders-first, the jumper's body passes over the bar while its centre of mass passes under it. Competitions raise the bar in stages, with three attempts per height and elimination after three straight failures. Jumpers may pass heights to save energy for bigger ones. Speed on the curve, power at take-off, and timing in the arch decide who clears what.

topics.History: The event dates to the first modern Games in 1896. The flop technique arrived in 1968 and became standard within a decade.
topics.Rules: Three attempts per height, elimination after three consecutive failures, and the bar rising in stages govern competitions.
topics.Techniques: A curved run-up, a powerful plant, and a timed back arch carry the jumper over. The centre of mass passes under the bar.
topics.Training: Curve sprinting, take-off drills, flexibility, and strength work build the jump.

title: Pole Vault
description: Sprint with a pole, plant it, ride its bend, and fly over a bar metres up: the pole vault is the most spectacular jump in athletics. Modern poles of fibreglass and carbon fibre are chosen by length and stiffness to fit the vaulter's speed and weight, and the pole's recoil does much of the lifting. The movement has distinct phases: plant, swing, rock-back, turn, and push-off, each timed to the pole's bend. Competitions raise the bar in stages with three attempts per height. Speed, strength, timing, and nerve all matter, and no other jump depends so much on equipment matched to athlete.

topics.History: The vault grew from practical pole crossing into Olympic competition, transformed by flexible fibreglass poles in the twentieth century.
topics.Rules: Three attempts per height, elimination after three consecutive failures, and a rising bar govern competitions.
topics.Techniques: The vault is a sequence: plant, swing, rock-back, turn, push-off. Pole stiffness and length must fit the vaulter.
topics.Training: Sprint work, pole drills, gymnastics strength, and short vaults build the event.

title: Shot Put
description: Push a heavy ball as far as you can, from inside a circle, without leaving it: that is the shot put. Men throw 7.26 kilograms and women 4 kilograms, and the ball must stay against the neck and shoulder until release. Two techniques dominate: the glide, sliding back across the circle, and the rotation, spinning to build speed before the push. Step outside the circle or over the stop board and the throw fouls. Power comes from the legs and hips, driven through a braced body into one explosive push. Several attempts decide it; the best legal throw wins.

topics.History: The event grew from stone putting into Olympic competition with standard weights: 7.26 kilograms for men, 4 kilograms for women.
topics.Rules: The shot must remain at the neck until release, and the thrower must stay inside the circle.
topics.Techniques: Glide or rotation builds speed; the release is a braced push, not a throw with the arm alone.
topics.Training: Throwing practice, heavy lifting, and explosive drills build the power the event needs.

title: Discus Throw
description: Spin across a circle and let a disc fly: the discus is the oldest throwing event still contested, and its beauty is rhythm. Men throw 2 kilograms, women 1 kilogram, and the discus must land inside a marked sector to count. The thrower builds speed through one and a half turns, keeping the discus flat so the air lifts it, then releases at an angle that carries it furthest. A cage surrounds the circle for safety, because a loose discus is dangerous. Balance through the spin matters more than brute strength; the smoothest throwers throw furthest.

topics.History: The discus is the oldest throwing event in the modern Games, present since 1896 and rooted in ancient competition.
topics.Rules: Sector landing, circle discipline, and standard weights govern the event. Throws outside the sector foul.
topics.Techniques: Rhythm through the spin, a flat discus, and a clean release carry the throw. Balance beats brute force.
topics.Training: Throwing practice, spin drills, and strength work build the event.

title: Hammer Throw
description: A metal ball on a wire, spun three or four times and released: the hammer throw is the most violent-looking event in athletics, and also one of the most controlled. Men throw 7.26 kilograms, women 4 kilograms, and the hammer orbits the thrower, pulling hard on arms and core. The thrower must stay balanced and relaxed through the turns, then release at exactly the right moment. A cage surrounds the circle, and sector rules apply as in the other throws. The winners are not the strongest athletes in the field; they are the ones who stay smooth while the hammer tries to pull them off their feet.

topics.History: The event grew from Celtic heavy events into Olympic competition with a standardised wire hammer.
topics.Rules: Sector landing and circle discipline govern throws; weights match the shot put at 7.26 and 4 kilograms.
topics.Techniques: Balance through three or four turns and a timed release decide throws. Relaxation under the hammer's pull is essential.
topics.Training: Throwing practice, turning drills, and core strength build the event.

title: Javelin Throw
description: Run, cross-step, and throw a spear further than anyone else: the javelin is the only throwing event from a runway, and it blends sprinting with throwing. Men throw 800 grams, women 600 grams, and the javelin must land tip-first inside the sector to count. The run-up builds speed, the cross-step sets the body, and the release over the shoulder sends the implement point-first into flight. Cross the foul line and the throw is lost. The best throwers are fast on the runway and clean at release; power alone, without timing, sends the javelin flat and short.

topics.History: The event descends from ancient spear throwing and has been Olympic since the early modern Games, with standardised implements.
topics.Rules: Tip-first sector landings count; foul-line crossings do not. Weights are 800 grams for men and 600 grams for women.
topics.Techniques: Runway speed, cross-step timing, and a clean release decide throws. A flat landing wastes the whole effort.
topics.Training: Throwing practice, sprint work, and shoulder strength build the event.
